analysis.one_liner: Ends state right-to-work laws nationwide by repealing the federal provision that allows them.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced September 4, 2025 with 17 Democratic cosponsors and was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The Nationwide Right to Unionize Act repeals section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the federal provision that lets states pass so-called right-to-work laws [S2]. Those state laws ban union security agreements — contracts that require workers to join the union or pay it fees as a condition of employment [S2]. Repealing 14(b) would override those state laws, letting unions and employers negotiate such agreements anywhere in the country. The bill has sat without action in the House Education and Workforce Committee since referral in September 2025 [S1][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Union members and workers who want to organize gain bargaining leverage: unions could require all workers covered by a contract to join or pay fees, which increases union funds and membership, and research links higher union density to better wages and benefits. Unions themselves gain members and dues revenue in states where such agreements are currently banned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Union members and workers seeking to organize

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, removing the federal authority states use to prohibit union security agreements [S2].

With state right-to-work bans preempted, unions and employers could negotiate contracts requiring membership or fee payment, strengthening union finances and bargaining power in the roughly half of states that currently ban such agreements [S2].
Sponsor Rep. Brad Sherman and 17 Democratic cosponsors introduced the bill, framing it as establishing a nationwide right to unionize [S1][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers in right-to-work states who do not want to join a union could be required to pay dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job. Employers lose the right-to-work environment many operate under, and could face higher labor costs and closer union oversight in organized workplaces.
analysis.who_pays_short: Non-union workers and employers in right-to-work states

drawbacks.text: Workers who decline to join a union could be forced to pay dues or agency fees as a condition of employment, overriding their choice [S2].
The bill overrides state laws that state legislatures — and in some states voters — enacted, raising a federalism objection that labor policy should be set state by state [S2].
Employers in currently right-to-work states could face higher labor costs and mandatory union arrangements, which opponents argue could discourage investment in those states [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want stronger unions, the bill removes the biggest legal barrier to union security agreements nationwide. The cost falls on workers who prefer not to fund a union and on employers in right-to-work states, who would lose that legal environment. The bill is a clean, single-provision repeal with no transition rules, so its effects would be immediate and nationwide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and has seen no further action [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced H.R. 5159 on September 4, 2025, joined by 17 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which holds jurisdiction over labor law [S4].
No markup, vote, or further action has occurred since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything material: the bill exists on paper only. Employers and right-to-work states keep the status quo for as long as the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and right-to-work states, so far

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the federal provision allowing state right-to-work laws [S1][S2].

for.name: 17 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors including Reps. McGovern, Nadler, Norton, Lynch, and Garamendi
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction [S3].

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no markup, no vote — since September 2025 [S4].

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: No Republican member cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee did not advance it [S3][S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee with no action [S3][S4].

industries.note: Unions could require membership or fees in every state, expanding membership and dues revenue. Union bargaining power is the mechanism by which the bill aims to lift wages for covered workers.

industries.industry: Employers (businesses with unionized or organizable workforces)
industries.note: Employers in right-to-work states would lose the ability to operate free of mandatory union arrangements and could face higher labor costs. In organized workplaces, employers would also gain a single bargaining partner covering all workers.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no action from the Republican-led Education and Workforce Committee in the months since referral, the bill is very likely to die in committee unless control of the House changes in the 2026 midterms. Labor-law repeals of this kind rarely reach the House floor in a divided Congress.
